definition.def: If you have doubt or doubts about something, you feel uncertain about it and do not know whether it is true or possible. If you say you have no doubt about it, you mean that you are certain it is true.
examples: This raises doubts about the point of advertising. [+ about/as to]
I had my doubts when she started, but she's getting really good.
They were troubled and full of doubt.
There can be little doubt that he will offend again.
Local inhabitants haven't the slightest doubt as to who is the rightful owner. [+ about/as to]

definition.def: If you doubt whether something is true or possible, you believe that it is probably not true or possible.
examples: Others doubted whether that would happen. [V if]
He doubted if he would learn anything new from Marie. [V if]
She doubted that the accident could have been avoided. [VERB that]

definition.def: If you doubt something, you believe that it might not be true or genuine.
examples: No one doubted his ability. [VERB noun]
Nobody that I spoke to doubted his sincerity as a politician. [VERB noun]

definition.def: If you doubt someone or doubt their word, you think that they may not be telling the truth.
examples: No one directly involved with the case doubted him. [VERB noun]
I still have no reason to doubt his word. [VERB noun]

definition.def: You say that something is beyond doubt or beyond reasonable doubt when you are certain that it is true and it cannot be contradicted or disproved. [emphasis]
examples: A referendum showed beyond doubt that voters wanted independence.
His ability is beyond any doubt.

definition.def: If you are in doubt about something, you feel unsure or uncertain about it.
examples: He is in no doubt as to what is needed. [+ about/as to]
When in doubt, call the doctor.

definition.def: You say I doubt it as a response to a question or statement about something that you think is untrue or unlikely.
examples: 'Somebody would have seen her.'—'I doubt it, not on Monday.'

definition.def: If you say that something is in doubt or open to doubt, you consider it to be uncertain or unreliable.
examples: The outcome was still in doubt.
That claim is increasingly open to doubt.

definition.def: You use no doubt to emphasize that something seems certain or very likely to you. [emphasis]
examples: The contract for this will no doubt be widely advertised.

definition.def: You use no doubt to indicate that you accept the truth of a particular point, but that you do not consider it is important or contradicts the rest of what you are saying.
examples: No doubt I'm biased, but it was the most cruel, evil human face I ever set eyes on.
No doubt many will regard these as harsh words, but regrettably they are true.

definition.def: If you say that something is true without doubt or without a doubt, you are emphasizing that it is definitely true. [emphasis]
examples: Without doubt this was the most important relationship I developed at college.
The refugees, without a doubt, are the most vulnerable.

definition.def: If you give someone the benefit of the doubt, you treat them as if they are telling the truth or as if they have behaved properly, even though you are not sure that this is the case.
examples: At first I gave him the benefit of the doubt.
Shalford is entitled to the benefit of the doubt.

definition.def: If you say that something is true without a shadow of a doubt or without a shadow of doubt, you are emphasizing that there is no doubt at all that it is true. [emphasis]
examples: It was without a shadow of a doubt the best we've played.

examples.sentence: It also reveals the power of the pauses and noises we use to play for time, convey emotion, doubt and irony.
No doubt the rats ate birds' eggs too.
The identity of the moai builders was in doubt until well into the twentieth century.

This questing nature of ours undoubtedly helped our species spread around the globe, just as it nowadays no doubt helps the last nomadic Penan maintain their existence in the depleted forests of Borneo, and a visitor negotiate the subways of New York.

The recordings revealed that bat activity over rice fields was much higher than it was in continuous forest - seven times higher over rice fields which were on flat ground, and sixteen times higher over fields on the sides of hills - leaving no doubt that the animals are preferentially foraging in these man-made ecosystems.
Roughly 11,700 years ago, as the most recent ice age ended, the climate became significantly warmer and wetter, no doubt making Obi's jungle much thicker.
There is no doubt that 'crimes against the person' rise in the summer, when the weather is hotter and fall in the winter when the weather is colder.
Such variation can no doubt be explained with reference to the habitats in which individual species have developed.
Not surprisingly, linguists doubt that any native speakers of Navajo will remain in a hundred years' time.
Some scientists doubt the value of traditional knowledge because the occupation of the Arctic doesn't go back far enough.
